interactive.title: The fixed arrow and the turning arrow
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Two pictures sit side by side. On the left, a 3 kN pull on a ring stays put. Its angle is the way the rope runs. On the right, an arrow turns round its tail once every cycle. Its height at each instant is its shadow on an upright line. That shadow traces a sine wave beside it. A freeze button stops it. Frozen, it is the fixed arrow you write as r∠θ. Its angle then marks a moment in the cycle. It is not a direction. Frozen at 45°, it is 2.5 ms into the cycle. On a 50 Hz supply, one turn takes 20 ms. The screens run like this. First come the two arrows, one still and one turning. A puzzle puts a current 90° behind the voltage. It asks how much later the current peaks. Next, two 3 kN pulls at 0° and 90° add nose to tail to 4.24 kN. Two 3 A currents a quarter turn apart add the same way, to 4.24 A. At every instant, the sum's height is their two heights added. Both arrows turn together, so their sum turns with them. A puzzle adds 6 A in step with the voltage to 8 A a quarter turn behind. Then a 50 Hz arrow and a 150 Hz arrow start together. The faster one gains. So the angle between them keeps changing. A puzzle asks how far apart they are after 5 ms. Next, a phasor is shown as a number. Divide the voltage by the current to get the impedance. You divide the sizes and take away the angles. So 230∠0° V ÷ 10∠−30° A gives 23∠30° Ω. A puzzle divides 230∠0° V by 5∠−60° A. After that, three phase currents leave a star point at 0°, −120° and 120°. Each one's size can be dragged. Beside them, the same arrows are laid nose to tail. Three equal 10 A currents close into a triangle. The neutral readout shows 0 A. Shorten one, and the chain falls short of closing. The gap is the neutral current, worked out by its parts. A puzzle has 10, 10 and 4 A. Two mixed puzzles end it. One has 10, 8 and 6 A. The other takes 230∠−120° V away from 230∠0° V. That gives the voltage between two lines. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn too. You can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The waves are pure sines at one frequency. Real electronic loads also draw harmonics. Some of those add up in the neutral, even on a balanced board. Each load is taken at the same power factor, so the three currents stay 120° apart. Loads at different power factors shift the angles too. The turning arrow is drawn at the wave's peak. So its shadow is the value at each instant. The three-phase arrows are drawn at rms. Shrinking every arrow by the same factor changes no angle. It does not change the shape of any sum either. The supply is taken as 50 Hz. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
A phasor is drawn like a vector and adds like one. But its angle marks a moment in time, not a direction in space. It is also a complex number, so you can divide it.

Start with a force arrow. A 3 kN pull on a ring points somewhere real. Its angle says which way the rope runs. Now take an arrow that turns round its tail once every cycle. Its height at each instant traces the sine wave of a voltage. Frozen at one instant, it is the fixed arrow you write as r∠θ. On a 50 Hz supply, one turn takes 20 ms. Say a current is 90° behind the voltage. It peaks a quarter turn later, 5 ms after the voltage. The angle measures that delay. Nothing in the cable points that way.

Turn two arrows together and their nose-to-tail sum turns with them. At every instant, the sum's height is the two heights added. That is why phasors add nose to tail, exactly as forces do.[^1] Take 6 A in step with the voltage and 8 A a quarter turn behind. Together they give √(6² + 8²) = 10 A, not 14 A. This only works when every arrow turns at the same speed. A 150 Hz arrow turns three times as fast as a 50 Hz one. So the angle between them changes from one instant to the next. They cannot share a diagram.[^2] Being a number gives a phasor one thing a vector lacks. You can divide one phasor by another. Ordinary vector rules give no way to divide one vector by another. To divide, divide the sizes and take away the angles. So 230∠0° V ÷ 10∠−30° A gives an impedance of 23∠30° Ω. But the dot product of two phasors does not give another phasor.[^3]

Three-phase is the ring of pulls again. Lay three equal currents 120° apart nose to tail, and they close into a triangle. What flows out on the lines must come back. So the neutral carries whatever the three lines do not cancel. On a closed chain, that is nothing. Now keep L1 and L2 at 10 A and shrink L3 to 4 A. The chain falls short of closing. The gap is the neutral current. The across parts give 10 − 5 − 2 = 3 A. The up parts give 0 − 8.66 + 3.46 = −5.20 A. So the neutral carries √(3² + 5.20²) = 6 A. A board with 10, 10 and 4 A sends 6 A back on the neutral, not 24 A. Its currents add as arrows. This is the ideal case of pure sine waves at one frequency. Real loads add harmonics, and some of those add up in the neutral.

**A phasor adds like a vector. Its angle is a shift in time, and as a number it can be divided.**

analogy.text: Picture two clocks on a bulkhead. One is set an hour behind the other. Their hour hands point 30° apart. That angle means an hour, not a direction. Both run at the same speed, so the gap stays 30° all day. Now fit one with a faster movement, and the gap drifts every minute. Waves of different frequencies drift apart in just that way.
analogy.breaks: A clock hand only tells the time. Its length means nothing. Two times never add to make a third. A phasor's length is the wave's size. And phasors add nose to tail.

practice.text:
Work it out on paper first. To check it on a live board, put a clamp meter round the neutral. Follow your safe system of work.

- Check that every wave has the same frequency. Only then can they share one diagram.
- Pick one phasor as the reference at 0°, such as L1's voltage. Measure every other phasor's angle from it.
- To add, lay the arrows nose to tail. Or add their across parts and their up parts.
- To take away, turn the second arrow round and add it.
- Find the size with Pythagoras. Find the angle with tan⁻¹, and check which quarter it lands in.
- To divide, divide the sizes and take away the angles.

**Rule of thumb:** Take pure sine currents 120° apart. Equal currents cancel, so the neutral carries nothing. When two lines carry the same current, the neutral carries the difference between that current and the third. With only one line loaded, the neutral carries all of its current. Harmonics from electronic loads can still add up in the neutral.

**Worked example:** Say L1 carries 20 A at 0°, L2 15 A at −120° and L3 10 A at 120°. Across: 20 − 7.5 − 5 = 7.5 A. Up: 0 − 12.99 + 8.66 = −4.33 A. The neutral carries √(7.5² + 4.33²) = 8.66 A. Its angle is tan⁻¹(−4.33 ÷ 7.5) = −30°. Adding the sizes would wrongly give 45 A.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the sizes. 10, 10 and 4 A leave 6 A on the neutral, not 24 A.
- Using the difference shortcut when all three differ. 10, 8 and 6 A leave 3.46 A, not 4 A.
- Drawing waves of different frequencies on one diagram. The angles between them drift.
- Reading a phasor's angle as a direction in the cable. It is a delay in the cycle.
- Adding when you should take away. The voltage between two 230 V lines is their difference, 398 V. Their sum is only 230 V.
- Multiplying V and I as complex numbers to get power. That adds their angles. True power uses the angle between them, in VI cos φ.

views.label: Drawn at the peak
views.text: The arrow is as long as the wave's peak. Its height at each instant is then the wave's value at that instant. The turning arrow is drawn this way.

views.label: Drawn at rms
views.text: The arrow is as long as the rms value a meter reads. The 230 V and three-phase arrows are drawn this way. Scaling every arrow alike changes no angle and no sum's shape.
